points: Saving reduces financial worry and gives the household security against unexpected costs.
A savings fund covers emergencies, such as job loss or an urgent repair, so the household does not have to borrow.
Regular saving allows the household to plan for expensive items or events, such as a holiday or a car.
Saving avoids the need for loans and credit agreements, and so avoids the interest charged on them.
Money held in a suitable scheme earns interest and grows over time.
Saving sets a good example for children and builds a sound financial reputation for the family.
Demand deposit account: money can be withdrawn on demand, so it suits short-term saving and an emergency fund.
Notice account: withdrawals require a set period of notice, and the interest paid is usually higher than on a demand deposit account.
Term deposit: money is locked away for an agreed period at a fixed rate, and early withdrawal usually reduces or loses the interest.
Regular saver account: a monthly deposit is made into an account that pays a higher rate in return for regular saving.
Instalment saving scheme: a fixed amount is saved each month for an initial period, and the money is then left to earn interest for a further period.
Savings certificates: a fixed-term product paying interest higher than an ordinary deposit account, with interest reduced if the certificate is cashed in early.
Savings bonds: a fixed-term product that pays interest at set intervals, with early withdrawal reducing or removing the interest earned.
A credit union is a member-owned, non-profit cooperative, and its share and saver accounts are run for its members.
Members can usually save small amounts regularly, and the credit union pays an annual dividend on savings.
Members with a savings record find it easier to qualify for a credit union loan.
Security: whether the savings are protected by a State or deposit guarantee, and how stable the institution is.
Interest: the rate paid, and the annual equivalent rate (AER), which shows the yearly return including the effect of compounding.
Compounding: interest is paid on earlier interest, so a longer-term deposit grows faster than the simple rate suggests.
Access: how quickly money can be withdrawn, and whether notice periods or penalties apply.
Tax: whether the interest is tax free, or subject to Deposit Interest Retention Tax (DIRT), which is deducted from interest on most bank and credit union deposits.
Purpose: short-term access for emergencies, and longer-term schemes for planned spending.

keyTerms.definition: A bank or credit union account from which money can be withdrawn on demand, usually with low interest.
A deposit account that requires a set period of notice before money can be withdrawn.
Money locked away for an agreed fixed period at a fixed rate, with interest lost or reduced on early withdrawal.
A fixed-term Post Office savings product with interest higher than a deposit account, reduced if cashed in early.
A savings account in a member-owned credit union, on which an annual dividend is paid.
The yearly interest rate including the effect of compounding, used to compare savings schemes.
A tax deducted from interest on most bank and credit union deposit accounts before the interest is paid.
Earning interest on both the original sum saved and the interest already added to it.

questions.prompt: Name one savings scheme suited to a family saving for a holiday within the next year, and explain how it meets the family's need for access to money.
questions.model: A named scheme such as a demand deposit account or a notice account. Access: a demand deposit account allows withdrawal on demand, so the money is available when the holiday is booked; a notice account needs notice to be given before money can be withdrawn. The scheme earns interest on the savings while they build up. A term deposit would lock the money away and reduce access.

questions.prompt: Compare a bank deposit account, a Post Office savings certificate and a credit union share account as savings schemes for a family, using security, interest, access and tax. Explain which of them would suit a family building an emergency fund.
questions.model: Security: each is a secure place to save, with protection of deposits depending on the institution and any State guarantee. Interest: the savings certificate pays more than an ordinary deposit account but is reduced if cashed in early; the credit union pays a dividend on savings; the bank account pays interest that depends on the account type. Access: the bank demand deposit and the credit union account allow withdrawal, while the certificate is locked for a term. Tax: interest on bank and credit union deposits is subject to DIRT, while savings certificate interest is tax free. A demand deposit or credit union account suits an emergency fund because the money can be reached quickly.
